## An e-mail you will get one day {.center}

> Hi! For the API connection, could you please send us **the certificate,
> the key and the password**? Thanks!

. . .

Should you send it? What *should* you send? What must you **never** send?

By the end of this session you'll know, and you'll be able to explain why.

::: notes
Ask for a show of hands: who would just send it? Don't give the answer yet;
we come back to this e-mail at the very end.
:::

## Today

1. **Secrets & fingerprints**: hashes and shared keys
2. **Key pairs**: padlocks, wax seals and mixing paint
3. **Trust**: certificates, who needs what, and red flags
4. **Exercises**, pick your track:
   - 🗣 **Explainers**: scenario cards, no terminal
   - 🛠 **Builders**: `openssl` in the sandbox

::: notes
Explainers are people who don't configure this themselves, but have to explain
to clients or third parties what is needed and why. Builders get their hands dirty.
:::

## Crypto does three jobs

| Job | The question | Everyday version |
|-----|--------------|------------------|
| 🔒 **Confidentiality** | Can anyone else read this? | A sealed envelope |
| 🧾 **Integrity** | Did anyone change this? | A tamper-evident seal |
| 🪪 **Authenticity** | Who am I *really* talking to? | A passport check |

. . .

Most "certificate problems" at work are really **authenticity** questions.

::: notes
Keep coming back to these three words. Every tool today does one or more of these jobs.
:::

# Part 1 · Secrets & fingerprints

## A hash is a fingerprint

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A["I owe you 10 euro"] --> H1(("SHA-256")) --> FA["f681…84cb"]
  B["I owe you 1000 euro"] --> H2(("SHA-256")) --> FB["a3f5…b3d1"]
```

- Same input → **always** the same fingerprint
- Tiny change → a **completely different** fingerprint
- There's **no way back** from the fingerprint to the document

::: notes
These are the real SHA-256 values; builders will reproduce them in exercise 1.
A hash is not encryption: there's no key, and nothing to decrypt.
Where you see them: download checksums, Git commits, certificate fingerprints,
and inside every digital signature.
:::

## One shared key: symmetric crypto 🏠

Like a **house key**: the same key locks and unlocks.

- **Fast**: gigabytes per second. It does the heavy lifting in TLS, VPNs and disk encryption
- **The catch**: how do you get a copy of the key to the other side
  without anyone copying it on the way?

::: notes
This is the key distribution problem. Hold that thought: Part 2 solves it.
:::

## Not all locks are equal

| Use today ✅ | Retired 🪦 |
|-------------|-----------|
| **AES-GCM** | DES, **3DES**: retired by NIST end of 2023 |
| **ChaCha20-Poly1305** | RC4: banned from TLS since 2015 |
| | AES-CBC without an integrity check: removed from TLS 1.3 |

. . .

GCM and Poly1305 are **AEAD**: a **tamper-evident envelope**.
Change one bit, and the recipient refuses the whole message.

::: notes
3DES has 64-bit blocks, which makes it vulnerable to the Sweet32 attack (2016).
ChaCha20 is fast on phones without AES hardware.
Builders will see in exercise 2 how an attacker changes "100 euro" into
"900 euro" in AES-CBC *without knowing the key*, and how AES-GCM refuses it.
:::

# Part 2 · Key pairs

## The padlock trick 🔓

Imagine you could hand out **open padlocks** for free.

- Anyone can snap one shut on a box and post it to you
- Only **you** have the key that opens them

. . .

That's public-key crypto:

- 🔓 **public key** = the open padlock → hand out as many as you like
- 🔑 **private key** = the only key that opens it → never leaves you

::: notes
The two keys are created together as a pair and are mathematically linked.
You can't work out the private key from the public key. That's the whole trick.
:::

## The golden rule {.center}

::: golden
**The private key stays home. The public key travels.**
:::

Anyone who has your private key *is you*, as far as computers are concerned.

::: notes
Say it twice. Everything in Part 3, and every red flag, follows from this one rule.
:::

## One key pair, two tricks

| | Encrypt 📦 | Sign ✍️ |
|---|---|---|
| **Goal** | Only the recipient can read it | Everyone can check it's from you, unchanged |
| **Done with** | the **recipient's public** key | **your private** key |
| **Opened / checked with** | the recipient's private key | **your public** key |
| **Everyday version** | the padlock | a wax seal only you own |

::: notes
A common mix-up: "I sign with the other party's key". No: you sign with your
own private key, and anyone can check it with your public key.
In practice, public-key encryption only protects a small symmetric key, and
the symmetric key does the bulk work (hybrid encryption).
:::

## Signing, step by step

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Alice (private key)
  participant B as Bob (Alice's public key)
  A->>A: fingerprint the contract (hash)
  A->>A: sign the fingerprint with her private key
  A->>B: contract + signature
  B->>B: fingerprint the contract himself
  B->>B: check the signature with Alice's public key
  Note over B: ✅ match: from Alice, unchanged<br/>❌ no match: changed, or not Alice
```

::: notes
A signature gives integrity and authenticity. It does NOT hide the content:
the contract travels in the clear.
"Only Alice could have made this" only holds if only Alice ever had the private
key. That's why it matters *who generates* a key pair (Part 3).
:::

## Agreeing on a secret in public: mixing paint 🎨

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false}}}%%
flowchart LR
  Y["🟡 common colour<br/>(public)"] --> AM & BM
  AS["🔴 Alice's secret"] --> AM["🟠 Alice's mix"]
  BS["🔵 Bob's secret"] --> BM["🟢 Bob's mix"]
  AM -- "sent in public" --> BF["🟤 Bob adds 🔵"]
  BM -- "sent in public" --> AF["🟤 Alice adds 🔴"]
```

Both end up with the same brown; an eavesdropper only sees 🟡 🟠 🟢 and can't un-mix paint.

::: notes
This is (EC)Diffie–Hellman, and it solves Part 1's "how do we share the house key?"
TLS does it for every connection, then switches to fast AES-GCM or ChaCha20.
"Ephemeral" (the E in ECDHE) means fresh paint for every connection. That gives
forward secrecy: stealing the server's key tomorrow does not unlock today's traffic.
:::

## RSA or elliptic curves?

| Algorithm | For ~128-bit security | Public key size | Notes |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|-------|
| **RSA** | 3072-bit key | 422 bytes | The veteran; encrypts *and* signs |
| **EC P-256** | 256-bit key | 91 bytes | Smaller and faster; ECDSA / ECDH |
| **Ed25519** | 256-bit key | 44 bytes | Modern signatures, hard to misuse |
: {tbl-colwidths="[16,26,22,36]"}

::: small
RSA-2048 is still everywhere (about 112-bit) and fine for now. **Coming up:
post-quantum** crypto. ML-KEM is already mixed into the TLS your browser uses today.
:::

::: notes
The sizes are the DER-encoded public keys builders will measure in exercise 3.
You don't need to remember numbers; remember "EC gives the same strength with
much smaller keys".
:::

# Part 3 · Trust

## But… whose padlock is it? 🤔

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Alice
  participant M as Mallory
  participant B as Bob
  A->>M: Bob, please send me your padlock
  M->>B: Bob, please send me your padlock
  B->>M: 🔓 Bob's padlock
  M->>A: 🔓 Mallory's padlock, "from Bob"
  Note over A: Alice locks her secret with Mallory's padlock 😱
```

Public keys are safe to share, **but you must know whose key it is**.

::: notes
The man in the middle. Encryption without authentication gives you a very
secure line to whoever answered the phone.
:::

## A certificate is a passport for a public key 🪪

- **Who**: a name: `shop.example`, or `Acme BV – API client`
- **What**: their **public key**
- **Allowed for**: **ServerAuth**? **ClientAuth**? (the Extended Key Usage)
- **Valid**: from … until …
- **Stamped by**: a notary, the **Certificate Authority (CA)**, who signed all of the above

. . .

No secrets inside → **a certificate is safe to share with anyone**.

::: notes
This is where the words ServerAuth and ClientAuth come from: they are fields
in the certificate saying what it may be used for.
A certificate alone proves nothing. In TLS the server also proves it holds the
matching private key by signing something fresh during the handshake.
:::

## The chain of trust

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false}}}%%
flowchart LR
  R["🏛 Root CA<br/>pre-installed or configured"] -- signs --> I["🏢 Intermediate CA"] -- signs --> L["🪪 shop.example"]
```

- You trust the **root**; the root vouches for the **intermediate**; the intermediate vouches for the **server**
- The server sends **its certificate + the intermediate(s)**
- The verifier must **already have the root** in its *trust store*

::: notes
Browsers and operating systems ship with roughly 150 public root CAs.
A *private CA* is your own notary's office: only systems that have had its
root certificate installed will trust it. Keep this in mind for the
"who needs what" slides.
:::

## Getting a passport: the CSR 📝

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false}}}%%
flowchart LR
  subgraph Owner["Owner of the key"]
    K["🔑 generate key pair"] --> C["📝 CSR<br/>public key + name"]
  end
  C -- "e-mail, portal: safe ✅" --> CA["🏛 CA checks & signs"]
  CA -- "certificate: safe ✅" --> Owner
```

The **private key never leaves its owner**, not even to go to the CA.

::: notes
CSR = Certificate Signing Request, the passport application form.
It contains the public key and the name, signed with the private key to prove
the applicant has it. It does not contain the private key.
:::

## Who needs what: ServerAuth 🌐

*"The clients check they're really talking to **our** server."*

| | Server owner (us) | Clients / third party |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Generates the key pair | ✅ | |
| Keeps the private key | ✅ never shared | |
| Sends a CSR to the CA, installs certificate + intermediates | ✅ | |
| Needs the CA's root certificate | | ✅ built in for a **public** CA<br/>**must be given it** for a **private** CA |
: {tbl-colwidths="[44,26,30]"}

::: notes
The usual support ticket: "your certificate is not trusted". With a public CA
that almost always means the server forgot to send the intermediate. With a
private CA the client doesn't have our root yet: send them the root CA
certificate, which is safe to share.
:::

## Who needs what: ClientAuth (mutual TLS) 🤝

*"Our server checks that it's really **Acme** calling."*

| | Acme (the client) | Us (the server checking) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Generates the key pair | ✅ on their own system | ❌ never for them |
| Keeps the private key | ✅ | |
| Gets a client certificate from | a CA we agreed on | |
| Needs the **issuing CA certificate(s)** | | ✅ as trust anchor |
| May also check | | the certificate's name or fingerprint |
: {tbl-colwidths="[38,30,32]"}

::: small
⚠️ Since **June 2026**, public CAs no longer issue certificates for ClientAuth.
Client certificates now come from a **private CA** (ours, Acme's, or a provider's).
:::

::: notes
Two common models:
(1) We run a private CA. Acme sends us a CSR, we sign it and send back the
certificate. We already trust our own CA.
(2) Acme has its own CA. They send us their CA certificate chain, and we trust
that CA, ideally only for Acme's specific name.
Either way, Acme generates and keeps the private key. If we generated it for
them, we could impersonate them, and "only Acme could have done this" no longer
holds.
The June 2026 change comes from the Chrome root program. "Just buy one at a
public CA" no longer works for mTLS.
:::

## Is this file safe to e-mail?

| File | Contains | Share? |
|------|----------|:------:|
| `.csr` | public key + name | 🟢 yes |
| `.crt` `.cer` | certificate | 🟢 yes |
| `ca.crt`, `chain.pem`, `ca-bundle` | CA certificates | 🟢 yes |
| `.key` | **private key** | 🔴 **never** |
| `.p12` `.pfx` | certificate **+ private key** | 🔴 **never** to another party |
| `.jks` | Java keystore, often with keys | 🔴 unless it's only CA certs |
| `.pem` `.der` | could be anything | 👀 look inside |

**Inside a `.pem`:** `BEGIN CERTIFICATE` 🟢 · `BEGIN CERTIFICATE REQUEST` 🟢 · `BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY` 🔴

::: notes
PEM is text (base64 between BEGIN/END lines); DER is the same bytes in binary.
File extensions are conventions, not guarantees, so open the file and look.
A password on a .p12 doesn't make it safe to e-mail: the password usually
arrives in the next e-mail.
:::

## Red flags 🚩

- *"Send us the private key / the .pfx and the password"*
- *"We'll generate the key pair for you and e-mail it"*
- *"Just turn off certificate verification for now"*
- *"It's self-signed, just click accept"*
- *"We use the same certificate and key for all our customers"*

Each one **breaks the golden rule** or **skips the "whose padlock?" check**.

::: notes
When is moving a .pfx OK? Inside one owner's own environment: you move your own
server certificate onto your own load balancer, over a secure channel. The
owner doesn't change. It's never OK when the key would go to another party.
:::

## Back to that e-mail

> …could you please send us **the certificate, the key and the password**?

. . .

> *"We're happy to send our **certificate and the CA chain**. The private key
> stays with us, so nobody else can pose as us. If you need to authenticate
> us as a client, tell us which **CA** you accept and we'll send you a **CSR**."*

::: notes
Ask the room what changed compared to the start. This template reply is also on the handout.
:::

## Recap

1. Crypto does three jobs: **secret**, **untampered**, **who**
2. Symmetric = one shared key, fast. Use **AES-GCM** or **ChaCha20-Poly1305**
3. **The private key stays home. The public key travels.**
4. Encrypt with *their* public key; sign with *your* private key
5. A **certificate** = public key + name, signed by a **CA**. Safe to share
6. The **owner** generates and keeps the key; the **verifier** needs the CA certificate
